slides.headline: No brain. No heart. No blood.
slides.sub: Jellies have got by like this for over 500 million years

slides.headline: A nerve net instead of a brain
slides.body: A loose web of neurons lets a jelly sense food, touch and light. Tiny balance organs tell it which way is up.

slides.label: of a jellyfish's body is water
slides.body: Only about 5% is solid matter. Most of the body is mesoglea, a thick jelly-like middle layer.

slides.headline: No heart, no blood, no problem
slides.body: A jelly is built from just three layers: an outer skin, the jelly middle and an inner digestive layer. There is no blood to pump.

slides.label: years since the oldest jelly ancestors lived
slides.body: Fossils show jellies in the Cambrian. Their ancestors may go back as far as 700 million years.

slides.headline: One tiny relative can run its life backwards
slides.body: The hydrozoan Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into a young polyp after reproducing, again and again. (It isn't the jelly pictured here.)

slides.headline: Proof you don't need a brain to last 500 million years.
slides.body: Send this to the friend who swears they'd never touch one.

caption:
No brain, no heart, no blood: moon jellies (Aurelia aurita) and their relatives are about 95% water.

Instead of a brain, a nerve net runs through the outer layer, the most basic nervous system known in a multicellular animal.One relative goes further. The tiny hydrozoan Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to a polyp after reproducing; its close cousin Turritopsis rubra cannot, and comparing their genomes points to differences in DNA repair and telomere-maintenance genes. The jellies in these photos are moon jellies (Aurelia aurita) and other species, not Turritopsis.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: NOAA Ocean Service; Smithsonian Ocean; Pascual-Torner et al., PNAS (2022).
